intro: Every stop of the talk ends with one action. These are the full plans behind them. Tools are named as examples, grouped by purpose — not endorsements.

roles.title: Universities & educators
roles.action: This term: change one assignment — AI allowed, explanation required.
blocks: This month — set the rule
Publish an AI rule for every assignment: a secure lane (AI-off, in person or oral) or an open lane (AI allowed and scaffolded) — e.g. the University of Sydney's two-lane model
Or label each task with the five-level AI Assessment Scale: No AI · AI Planning · AI Collaboration · Full AI · AI Exploration
Every lecturer runs a coding agent on their own assignment and notes what it gets right and wrong
This term — change the evidence
Pick one assignment per course and add a 5-minute oral defence, a planted-bug review, a live change request (15 minutes, AI allowed, explained afterwards) and a process log
Use the rubric in section (e) and calibrate it across staff with three sample submissions
Teach the Keep · Shift · Add · Prove model explicitly to students
This year — change the course
AI-off checkpoints in foundation courses; an agentic capstone in the final year
A monthly staff community of practice: share assignments, rubrics and failures
Compare grades with oral-defence results to see where the old assessment over-graded
Update the syllabus: keep the core, shift the weight, add agentic workflows and AI-aware security

roles.title: Students
roles.action: One project: build it by hand, extend it with an agent, explain every line.
blocks: The myth — “AI does everything, so I don't need to learn”
Wrong. Less of: memorising syntax, typing boilerplate, hunting through API docs
More of: engineering — design, debugging, testing, security, reading & reviewing code
You still read and understand every line — and write it yourself when needed
Good news: learning a new concept has never been faster. The catch: there's more to learn
Foundations — the engineering core
Know how an OS runs your code: processes, memory, threads, files
Model data and write real SQL: schemas, joins, indexes, transactions
Design with OOP — not just classes: responsibilities, interfaces, composition
Solve the problem before you prompt: decompose it and sketch it, then ask
Programming, data structures & algorithms; HTTP & APIs; Git, testing and debugging; auth basics and the OWASP Top 10
See the whole SDLC: requirements → design → build → test → deploy → operate
Breadth — go broad, not narrow
Be a product engineer — own a feature end to end: the user problem, UI, API, data, tests, release. It's a way of working with product and design; it doesn't replace analysts or testers
Learn a business domain (fintech, health, e-commerce…): domain understanding is what AI can't supply
Keep one deep strength (T-shaped), but don't define yourself by a single layer or framework
Edge — what sets you apart
Technical English — a prompt is a specification; write it clearly in English: inputs, outputs, constraints, acceptance criteria
GenAI & agents — after you can code: by hand → with AI → with agents. Agentic coding is a skill too — learn it after you've written code yourself
Read code you didn't write — and review AI output like a teammate's pull request
Learning order
1 · Write it yourself
2 · Use AI to explain, compare and critique
3 · Delegate to agents — once you can verify the result
Weekly habits
First version by hand — AI may explain, not solve
Log what the AI got wrong — and how you noticed
Teach back one concept a week: a post, a talk or a study partner
A 30-minute AI-off kata: an algorithm, a bug or a small refactor
Concepts outlive tools — learn the concept behind each tool
Framework APIs → separation of concerns
ORM syntax → data modelling & transactions
AI coding products → decomposition & validation
Cloud commands → scalability & reliability
Security libraries → authN/authZ & threat modelling
Frameworks change. Engineering principles travel with you.
Portfolio project — one small API, built twice
v1 by hand: a small REST API with auth, a database and tests
v2: extend it with a coding agent — one new feature, end to end
Ship a README, an AGENTS.md (your rules for the agent) and a process log
Negative tests for every auth rule, and a short “3 AI mistakes I caught” write-up
A 5-minute walkthrough video that explains every design decision
Ready when
You can build and debug a small service with AI off — and explain the version you built with AI

roles.title: Fresh graduates & juniors
roles.action: Make it visible: every PR explained, every agent mistake logged.
blocks: Stand out — before day one
One project with a process log and an AGENTS.md
One merged open-source pull request
An “AI mistakes I caught” write-up
Be ready to explain every line — and to change it live
Breadth on the job — everything from Stop 03 applies
The Students plan is yours too: foundations, breadth (the product-engineer mindset) and edge
Volunteer for cross-stack tickets — breadth, on the job
Learn the business domain of your first product: ask why each feature exists
Days 1–30 — learn the system
Set up your agent with the team's context files and conventions
Read the codebase with AI as a guide; draw the architecture yourself
Fix three small bugs — first attempt by hand, then compare with the agent
Days 31–60 — contribute
Issue → plan → agent → verify → PR, with the plan approved before the code
A negative test with every change
Pair with a senior on one agent session; ask them to review your prompts and diffs
Days 61–90 — own
One small feature, end to end
A written design rationale: two alternatives considered, and why this one
Catch one bug before review — and write down how you found it

roles.title: Experienced software engineers
roles.action: This sprint: review one agent session as a team — and do one task AI-off.
blocks: Developer
Master one agent end to end: issue → approved plan → PR, with your own verification
A weekly AI-off kata; own the regression tests
Ready when you catch agent errors before reviewers do
Senior
Own the guardrails and the context: AGENTS.md, hooks, review rules
Threat-model AI-generated changes
Coach juniors through their agent sessions — plans, prompts and diffs
Ready when the teams around you produce better AI-assisted work
Lead / architect
Publish team AI standards and update the competency matrix
Measure stability as well as throughput
Make agent-session review part of mentoring and promotion
Ready when the team ships faster, stability holds and juniors grow judgment
New ways of learning — every level
Pair with an agent: state the intent, approve the plan, review every diff
Practise AI-off: one kata or debugging session a week
Review agent sessions as a team, like code review
Write the context every agent on the team reads

roles.title: Engineering leaders
roles.action: Rewrite one development plan around what people can safely own.
blocks: Development plans

Replace “complete an AI course” with a demonstrable outcome: deliver one agent-assisted repository-level change, show the context and constraints you gave the agent, and independently validate the result against defined acceptance criteria
Mentoring
Review agent sessions — plan, prompts, diffs — and ask people to explain the change back
Manage juniors for learning, not production (Kent Beck)
Promotion
Delegation radius · decision quality · defects caught before review · people grown — not output volume

roles.title: Software companies & teams
roles.action: Start Monday: baseline first — then adopt, train and measure together.
blocks: Days 1–30 — foundations
A clear, communicated AI stance and guardrails: data, security, review rules
Two or three workflows, with pilot teams
Baseline delivery and quality (lead time, change failure rate, escaped defects) before rollout
Context files in key repositories
Days 31–60 — capability
Training by career stage, not a one-off workshop — BCG: regular use is sharply higher with at least five hours of training
Mentoring through agent-session reviews
Update onboarding and one competency row
Days 61–90 — measure & scale
Compare with the baseline across delivery, quality and capability — not seats or % AI-generated code
Scale or stop each workflow on evidence
Update development plans and promotion criteria
Use as a checklist
DORA AI Capabilities Model: clear AI stance · healthy data ecosystems · AI-accessible internal data · strong version control · small batches · user-centric focus · quality internal platforms

roles.title: Software buyers & stakeholders
roles.action: Ask your vendor how they use AI — and how they verify it.
blocks: Within your reach
Simple apps you build yourself: prototypes, internal tools and automations
What agentic AI changes
Teams deliver faster and at lower cost — delivery cycles shrink when engineers direct agents well
What it doesn't change
It's still engineering: security, integration, data, scale and support take expertise, time and budget
